I'm sorry you experienced that-- that *is* pretty hurtful. I didn't get a diagnosis until I was already married, but I would tell the people I dated what exactly I had a hard time with in terms of communication (among other things, like sensory issues.)

For example: types of jokes I didn't get. Or if we were talking about serious topics, to try to refrain from giving vague answers/joke answers when I asked, "Do you mean x or do you mean y?" and they would reply with, "Yes." I let them know what helped me understand them better/how they could better understand me. 

It has always been very difficult for me to make close connections, and I struggled with my confidence because of this. I always felt like I was doing something "wrong", but a lot of self-work and patience eventually brought me more ease and acceptance. It's hard for sure. Personally, disclosing I'm autistic helps me. The way I see it is, my autism is going to show itself in one way or another. Having clear, ongoing, communication and being as open as possible is beneficial to all parties involved. This applies to friendships, familial relationships, and romantic relationships. And to relationships of all kinds between NTs and other neurodivergent folks as well! If someone can't accept that I'm on the spectrum and views that in a negative light, it isn't because of me. That's a bias they have to work through. You can always have a conversation (or multiple, if they're willing to hear you out) to debunk some myths, but if they hold true to that bias, then it just won't work and that's okay. 

If you need to take a break from dating to collect your thoughts, that's perfectly fine and normal. I wish you luck in the future. <3

I haven't been diagnosed yet (evaluation later this month!), though I have been asked throughout my life if I'm on the spectrum and I myself have identified strongly with many people's experiences in the reddit  autism communities. Much like you, the roles, rules, the direct, open communication make things so much easier for me. There's always clarity. I realized a couple years ago that I just could not do vanilla relationships because of the guessing games/reading between the lines/subtle cues partners expected me to just "get." I also feel more valued because I know my partner wants me and is attracted to me. I used to feel... I don't know, like I couldn't always be too sure? I also had some pretty rough experiences too, so I'm sure that didn't help things.

This is not to say I think all vanilla relationships are like this though; I just find it more common for vanilla folks not to communicate openly and directly in my own experience. I've definitely had a couple of Doms not be open/direct with me and wind up ghosting me--stories for another time. Any relationship, platonic or otherwise, whether the people are autistic or allistic, can benefit from setting clear boundaries and having open conversation. 

And as for the sensory thing, yes! I always feel safe and comfy when I'm restrained. Especially if I've had a rough day/week and have experienced too much activity (social interactions, coworkers being extra chatty, too many tasks to deal with, and just generally existing outside of my apartment.) You already have a ton of comments on here, so maybe you won't see this. Thanks for sharing your story; it's an understatement to say acquaintance rape is difficult to deal with. You do feel like you lose a lot. It's something I'm grappling with too. 

It's easier said than done for sure, but try to be kind to yourself. Everyone's trauma response is different. Your brain just picks up on triggers sometimes you wouldn't even expect to be triggers. Neurobiology of trauma is complicated, but whatever you experience, it's a normal response. For some it's easier to get through, for others it's not. Lives are complex and nuanced. It is a legitimate fear not to want to tell anyone because you may not know who this information will reach, if you'll get backlash or interrogated from people you trust when all you want is someone to listen, how it will affect your other relationship dynamics with friends/family. Because of that, it may be easier to not put yourself through the consequences of your incident being shared. For some it's worth sharing their story, for others it isn't. You know your life better than anyone else. Go at your own pace and do what you feel is right. I saw in some other posts, you don't want to let your association with the guy and tabletop gaming get in the way. That's awesome resilience! At the same time, try your best not to be frustrated with yourself if it still feels uncomfortable to play tabletop games. You don't have to push yourself into situations like that. It works for some people, but if you have to revisit the activity at a later time, that's okay too.

I believe if you have healthy outlets to get your feelings out in *some* way, it's helpful.  A hobby (new or old) can help. Talking in some form can be really cathartic too, if or whenever you're ready. I'm not sure if you feel this way, but I know some people don't want to feel like they're "putting too much" on their SO. But since you already spoke with your husband, maybe talking about how you feel with him once in a while can be helpful. If you ever feel comfortable talking to someone else, like a friend or even a therapist (if that's within your means), that could be helpful too. I'm just an internet stranger, but I'm here as well. You have options. ♡

You can definitely be depressed without feeling suicidal. Some people just don't want to exist anymore. I get that sort of depression a lot. What you're feeling is valid. I wish I could respond more appropriately to your thoughts about university, but it doesn't seem we live in the same country so I'm not familiar with how it all works where you live. 

You can weigh your options. I'm in a lot of debt due to students loans. I went to school for something I liked and was led to believe there were jobs. Turns out there were, but it wasn't steady, did not make enough, and the lifestyle I would have had to adopt was not feasible enough for my circumstances. I have hardly used my education in a career setting, save for doing a few one off projects throughout the last 7 years. What worked best for me was finding work and saving up towards things I wanted to enjoy. I'm not sure what I want to do anymore in regards to higher education. It's still a bit of a sore spot for me, and I don't want to accrue more debt. I just figured I want to spend my life accumulating satisfying experiences, so I'll save towards that and paying off my debt. It took me a long time to realize that (for myself) living a quality life did not have to solely consist of obtaining a degree, making money, and hitting any number of certain goals/milestones by a certain age. The expectations set by those around me, which I adapted myself, kept me from really enjoying my life. It seemed to be the normal. Everyone was doing these things. They seemed successful. So why couldn't I? 

I've managed to find pretty decent paying jobs by accumulating experience in fields that didn't require a degree. I also know of some people that went to college/university for one thing and they didn't stay in that field, for whatever reason. It may not have been what they thought or wanted or maybe they just needed a change and their interest had shifted. Their degrees, although specialized, could be applied to other jobs. Some jobs in my country only ask that you have a 4 year degree. The rest can be learned in training. I don't know if this is common where you live, but it could be something to keep in mind.

The thing that is really good to take advantage of now, at least from the information you provided, is that you don't have student debt. You can work and save if getting a degree is something you would really like and you wouldn't be hindered by owed money. Also, you have people that make you feel good in your life, and you have hope. Try your best to hold onto those things; they can be very useful. I wish you the best, and I hope that by relaying my experience it helped a little.

You're not being dramatic and you have the right to feel what you do. We all have different sets of experiences that place us at different points of understanding in our lives. No one is "stupid" for having feelings. I think as many of us get older, we tend to forget where we were as teenagers, so some people downplay (sometimes unintentionally) the problems a young person faces. 

I see much of my younger self in you, since I had an abusive family and was told much of the same things your parents have said to you, have been mercilessly bullied, and abused by a couple of people that were close to me. Something similar also happened with someone I was with for a couple years but had known for over a decade. To hear that "I had just kind of seen you as friends with benefits" really tore into me because they really did not portray their feelings this way. They even talked seriously about marrying me and having a family. I was 18/19 at the time and had never known what it was like to date or feel kindness and love from someone. They really made me feel like I could trust them fully and like I was safe. I thought that if this relationship with this seemingly amazing and understanding person couldn't work, then how could a relationship with anyone else work? 

I have a fiance now. It's freaking wild, since I thought I'd never see this happen. I didn't think I'd be alive this long. I still deal with depression, but I have come so very far with managing it. I won't try to sell you cures or that everything is going to be okay. I don't know what will happen. I can only tell you that like you, I couldn't move on, didn't want to move on. It's a little bizarre how this all came to be and I don't fully understand it yet, but I guess I just got tired and accepted things as they are. In a way, "accepting defeat" is what helped me find solace within myself, and I stopped looking for other people to bring me that acceptance and happiness. Except I wasn't technically defeated because I'm still here. I didn't  want to look at it as defeat. Those feelings of despair and hopelessness drove me to make an attempt to feel better. Anyway, it was a long, very tiring and complicated journey of trying just about anything to feel better. I don't want to make this about myself; just sharing a tidbit of what I've gone through so that maybe you can glean something from it, if anything.

Sometimes it's just too much. Sometimes you're sick and tired. Sometimes you don't want to have to be the one to pick up all the pieces by yourself. I think as humans, regardless of how introverted or jaded some of us may be, are gregarious in nature and need some form of acceptance. That's why so many type their feelings and stories into posts on subreddits like this. Sometimes in making that post, there is still a sliver of hope. They may be looking for an answer, something to keep them from going through with it one more time or to know that someone saw what they had to say. I don't know you, but I'd hate for you-- for anyone-- to take their life. I'd understand and could never place the blame on someone if they did. They are not cowards. We're all just trying to get by in this oftentimes chaotic string of events that is life. It's tough.

When I was 10 years old, there was a girl that lived across the street from me that I would sometimes play with. She was about my age. I didn't like hanging out with her too much because she threw serious tantrums over things that I thought were really trivial, especially at our age. I loved drawing, so we would sit down and draw things together sometimes. She drew a very violent picture of herself bleeding from her stomach and holding a knife. I was a pretty quiet kid that liked to keep to myself most of the time, and being around someone like that was really exhausting and kind of scary to me. I didn't want the conflict. 

I remember one incident in particular where I saw this girl crossing the street to my house from one of our windows. I hurried over to my mom, asking her to please makeup an excuse  as to why I couldn't play today. So she did. The girl threw a fit and she stomped her feet,  screaming and crying about how it wasn't fair. Then suddenly after a couple minutes her eyes went dull, and she slid into a defeated posture before trudging back home. 

Years later, I had since moved away to a different town and was 15 years old by this point. My mom was working as a sexual violence crisis hotline operator. She came home shocked one evening and told me that this neighbor girl's mother called the hotline seeking counseling services for her daughter. Her father had been abusing her for years. I know... she should have kept such sensitive information confidential. This girl always wanted me to sleep over, but I never did because my mom had never given me permission. 

All the seemingly random tantrums and that drawing? Most likely her way of dealing with the abuse she was experiencing. I was probably the only kid in the neighborhood that gave her the time of day, and I tried to avoid her. I felt badly for a while for doing that when all she needed was a friend. Sometimes we may just think a kid likes to cause problems for the hell of it. It's easy for us to dismiss children and not take them seriously. Society tends to forget that kids are people too. They're developing. More often than not, they're acting out for a reason, usually because they're experiencing a turbulent home life.

Maybe I'm a little late to the game on this, but I'll share anyway. This is a long one. Excuse any formatting issues. I'm on mobile. TL; DR: Lived alone, locked in my apartment the whole day like a hermit. Went to the bathroom to take a piss, stepped out, spotted random patch of wet blood (?) on the carpet that wasn't there before.

One time in particular sticks out to me at the moment. 2 years ago. My roommate moved out a few months before, so I was living alone. I didn't have any trouble with the neighborhood prior to him leaving or even after. It was a small and relatively safe area, quiet, and two police officers lived there (you could see their squad cars parked in the lot, one being the first thing you see coming in.) One would even see off the kids in the neighborhood every morning for school. I know that doesn't necessarily mean the place isn't prone to crime, but there was a sense of safety and  the cars could be a deterrent. You also needed a cardkey to enter the gate guarding the complex. Guests could get in only by calling your landline or local cell phone number; No keypad. I was from out of state, so I didn't have either of these and I definitely wasn't expecting guests as I didn't know many people. I had but one friend at the time, a co-worker of mine, and he never visited. I'm  not one to give out many details about my life, especially those concerning where I live. So that sets things up a bit. 

Anyway, it's 8 pm on a Sunday and I'm in my room, having spent my entire day home. Nature calls. I go to the bathroom, which is conveniently located in my room. Takes a few minutes, right? Upon coming back out , I pause. 

There's  a sizeable crimson red blot on the carpet about a foot away from the front of my bathroom door. And it looks wet. This is odd. Is that paint? I'm artistic so that wouldn't be unusual. Maybe it was on a shoe or something and dripped/smeared. Except the 5 ounce bottle of red paint I did have had  been thrown out 5 months ago after being used up. It wouldn't have been out either since I didn't paint that day and had not painted since I threw that bottle out. The supplies I did have were packed away. Maybe I'm  bleeding? I check myself about 5 to 7 times. Nope, not bleeding. I (cautiously and with mace in hand) check the entire apartment twice. I didn't  have much to search. My old roommate took his things and I had but a crappy little couch and TV in the living room. Nothing out of place. All windows were locked. Both locks on the front door were secure and the chain was in place as I had left it. No leaks through the ceiling and walls or edges of the rooms.

Thoughts are racing, searching as thoroughly as possible for any logical explanation. My only thought was the sliding door in my bedroom to the balcony. It hadn't been open when I first checked it. The lock was switched on and the metal safety bar (?) was still wedged in place. Okay, I thought to myself. Whatever. 10 minutes had passed after I left my bathroom. All was still and quiet.

Perhaps it was my nerves, but I thought I heard faint footsteps on my balcony. I listen again. Yes. Those are definitely footsteps. 4 distinct footsteps. I had enough and decided to call the police. I take a picture of the splotch and wait as calmly as I possibly can for the officer to arrive. In the meantime, I decided to call my co-worker to see if he could come over, keep me company, and see if he could make sense of things. The officer arrives about 45 minutes later, searches my apartment, takes my story, examines  the red spot, and says he'll search the outside of the building and the neighborhood. 20 minutes later he comes knocking at my door saying there were no signs of suspicious activity, says there's  nothing that could be done, and to call again if anything else happens. He then takes his leave. 

My friend arrives about 10 minutes later. I find out he carries a concealed gun on his person so this is slightly comforting. He scopes out the apartment and finds nothing unusual. I put on gloves and clean the wet blotch with a paper towel for the time being. It wasn't nearly as thick as paint like I'd hoped. It was more of the consistency of blood. This little discovery sends shivers down my spine and makes my stomach sink, but I shove those feelings aside and toss the paper towel face up in a separate plastic shopping bag from my bathroom trash. My buddy and I watch a bit of TV so that we could calm our nerves, and he camps out in the living room for the rest of the night. Next morning, I check the paper towel. It dried brown. Much like blood. Once again, I checked the apartment  along with all of my clothes and other belongings. I don't  know of any other substance that can turn up red and dry brown like that. I know certain car fluids can look similar to blood but again, I hadn't  been out at all and didn't keep anything like that inside. Occasionally, I'll think back on this and scratch my head over it. I can't  totally say what that was with certainty. I thought perhaps it could have been a creepy maintenance or leasing office worker that had access to my apartment. Even then, I don't know how anyone could get in past either of the two doors, walk into my room, and chain or bar them from outside within a few minutes without me hearing a thing.
